e-5616.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
e-5616.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/c3d64ddcfd33db2e96caf6db5d85587857c3715e8d91a7dc8f4801c117fc89b0.png) 
and the vectors 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/4fbbb82838d7fa94fe0aeb47ed48952bfe573e12874d3891f8650a15b46e0ee7.png)
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $\mathbf{T}?$
e-5616.worked_solution:
A vector $\mathbf{u}$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ if $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_i)$ for each vector $\mathbf v_i\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)=\mathbf{0},$ we conclude that, of the given vectors, the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,\mathbf{T}$ is $\,\mathbf{v}_1.$

e-5441.knowledge_point: Calculating a Component of a Vector in the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
e-5441.problem: Consider the linear transformation ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/d0a0fabd7275cdceed8c0c62e58bbfc0e5f23322145d551e412877075cbb6e3c.png) and the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/4dd5f4c300c5870e696c5485fffdef1bbd9b7741b23c7d27fda1198e31baa33b.png) Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,\mathbf{u}\in\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}).$
e-5441.worked_solution:
A vector $\mathbf{u}$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ if $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}3\cdot k+12\cdot 2-3\cdot 6 \\ -2\cdot k+4\cdot 2-2\cdot 6 \\ 6\cdot k-3\cdot 2+3\cdot 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3k+6 \\ -2k-4 \\ 6k+12\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}3k+6=0 \\ -2k-4=0 \\ 6k+12=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to all three of these equations is $k=-2.$

e-5439.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
e-5439.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\mathbf{T}$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/5fa2e7ff6cfc27fce7698124fb835abf5c6f02221ba7c7ebb0b371fef6d3c15a.png)

Setting ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/f9fc80048a348773c656ec98ac9299eb1c611bfb07eee747b883eb7398dc295f.png) we then need to solve the equation $T\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x,$ and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-2y.
$$

 

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,\mathbf{T}$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/cace77f13c7ef817cfefaab742bdca008b29a177b0783dc761bc24d8a1273af3.png)

e-5440.knowledge_point: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
e-5440.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/f27d3195556ff8786f9416cddbe4ad52cf1838f2b0ce37b4da11746fee59fb9c.png)

Recall that $\textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = \textrm{nullity}(T) = \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 10 & -1 \\ -6 & -12 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -6 & -12 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot columns. Therefore, 

$$
\textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T})=\textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T))=0.
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Consider the linear transformation
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}6x-4y \\ 2x-y \\ -5x+3y\end{aligned}]$ and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
after.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 4 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{i})\ne 0$ for any $i$'s, we conclude that none of them belongs to the kernel of $\,T.$

after.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each vector ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{2})=0,$ we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,T$ is ${v}_{2}.$

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4x+2y \\ 6x+3y\end{aligned}]$ 
and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6\end{aligned}],{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}].$
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $T?$
content.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each vector ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{2})=0,$ we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,T$ is ${v}_{2}.$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the linear transformation
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+4y \\ y+z \\ x-4z\end{aligned}]$ and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
after.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$

Question 4

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[x+4yy+zx−4z] and the vectors v1=[4−11],v2=[−41−1],v3=[000]. Which of the given vectors belong to Ker(T)?

a
v2 and v3 only
b
v1 only
c
v1 and v3 only
d
v1, v2, and v3
e
v1 and v2, only
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A vector u belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation T if T(u)=0.

Therefore, we need to compute T(vi) for each vi: T(v1)=T([4−11])=[000]T(v2)=T([−41−1])=[000]T(v3)=T([000])=[000]

Since T(v1)=T(v2)=T(v3)=0, we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of T are v1, v2, and v3.

verification.explanation: Substitution gives T(v₁)=T(v₂)=T(v₃)=(0,0,0), agreeing with the revealed solution. All three vectors belong to the kernel, including the zero vector.

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem:
Consider the linear transformation
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+4y \\ y+z \\ x-4z\end{aligned}]$ and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
content.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$

b
v2 and v3 only
c
v2 only
d
v1 and v2 only
e

decision.explanation: A vector belongs to the kernel when its image is zero. T(v₁)=(-2,12,0), T(v₂)=(12,-9,0), and T(v₃)=(0,0,0). Therefore only v₃ belongs to the kernel.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-4y+4z \\ -5x+10y-3z \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ 
and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}],{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$
Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
after.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 12 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}10 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -9 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,T$ is $\,{v}_{3}.$

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[2x−4y+4z−5x+10y−3z0] and the vectors v1=[121],v2=[1053],v3=[210]. Which of the given vectors belong to Ker(T)?

a
None of the given vectors belong to the kernel of T
b
v2 and v3 only
c
v2 only
d
v1 and v2 only
e
v3 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A vector u belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation T if T(u)=0.

Therefore, we need to compute T(vi) for each vi:

T(v1)=T([121])=[−2120]T(v2)=T([1053])=[12−90]T(v3)=T([210])=[000]

Since T(v3)=0, we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of T is v3.

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-4y+4z \\ -5x+10y-3z \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ 
and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}],{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$
Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
content.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 12 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}10 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -9 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,T$ is $\,{v}_{3}.$

choices.value: None of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $T$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-y+z \\ -6x+3y-3z \\ 4x-2y+2z\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ k\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
after.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}2\cdot 3-1+k \\ -6\cdot 3+3\cdot 1-3\cdot k \\ 4\cdot 3-2\cdot 1+2\cdot k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5+k \\ -15-3k \\ 10+2k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}5+k=0 \\ -15-3k=0 \\ 10+2k=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to all three of these equations is $k=-5.$

The solution to both of these equations is $k=-6.$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-8x+4y \\ 6x-3y \\ 2x-y\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ k \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
after.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}-8\cdot 3+4\cdot k \\ 6\cdot 3-3\cdot k \\ 2\cdot 3-k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-24+4k \\ 18-3k \\ 6-k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-24+4k=0 \\ 18-3k=0 \\ 6-k=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to all three of these equations is $k=6.$

Question 11
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[−9x−3y+3z−12x−4y+4z6x+8y+10z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[z−2zz]:z∈R}
b
{[−13z−3zz]:z∈R}
c
{[y+zyz]:y,z∈R}
d
{[xx−2zz]:x,z∈R}
e
{[xy2x−3y]:x,y∈R}
Submit

decision.explanation: Setting T(x,y,z)=0 gives 3x+y-z=0 and 6x+8y+10z=0; the second output equation repeats the first constraint. Substituting y=z-3x into the remaining equation gives -18x+18z=0, so x=z and y=-2z. Thus the kernel consists exactly of (z,-2z,z) for real z.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z \\ -12x-4y+4z \\ 6x+8y+10z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
after.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=-2z.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z & =0 \\ -9x-3(-2z)+3z & =0 \\ -9x+9z & =0 \\ x & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is ${[\begin{aligned}z \\ -2z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R}.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[−9−33−12−446810].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−9−33−12−446810]R2:=R2+(−43)R1∼[−9−330006810]R3:=R3+23R1∼[−9−330000612]R2↔R3∼[−9−330612000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z \\ -12x-4y+4z \\ 6x+8y+10z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
content.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=-2z.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z & =0 \\ -9x-3(-2z)+3z & =0 \\ -9x+9z & =0 \\ x & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is ${[\begin{aligned}z \\ -2z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R}.$

before.html:
Question 12
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[2x−4y+2zx−3y+z4x−4y+z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[−yy0]:y∈R}
b
{[000]}
c
{[y−2zyz]:y,z∈R}
d
{[x1z]:x,z∈R}
e
{[110]}
Submit

decision.explanation: Setting T(x,y,z)=0, the first equation divided by 2 gives x-2y+z=0. Subtracting the second equation gives y=0, so z=-x. The third equation then gives 4x+z=3x=0. Thus x=y=z=0, and the kernel contains only the zero vector.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-4y+2z \\ x-3y+z \\ 4x-4y+z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
after.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x,$ $y,$ and $z.$ From the third equation, we obtain $z=0$ and from the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is ${[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.$

Question 12
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[2x−4y+2zx−3y+z4x−4y+z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[−yy0]:y∈R}
b
{[000]}
c
{[y−2zyz]:y,z∈R}
d
{[x1z]:x,z∈R}
e
{[110]}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[2−421−314−41].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[2−421−314−41]R1↔R2∼[1−312−424−41]R2:=R2+(−2)R1R3:=R3+(−4)R1∼[1−3102008−3]R3:=R3+(−4)R2∼[1−3102000−3]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-4y+2z \\ x-3y+z \\ 4x-4y+z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
content.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x,$ $y,$ and $z.$ From the third equation, we obtain $z=0$ and from the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is ${[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-6x+y \\ 12x-2y\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 12 & -2\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 12 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=\frac{1}{6}y.
$$

 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{aligned}]y,\,y\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[−6112−2].

Setting x=[xy], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−6112−2]R2:=R2+2R1∼[−6100]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x, and we have one free variable, y. That means we need to find x in terms of y.

From the first equation, we get x=16y.

Therefore, if x∈Ker(T), then

x=[16yy]=[161]y,y∈R.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms x=y/6, so the kernel is spanned by the nonzero vector (1/6,1). Its image is (-1+1,2-2)=(0,0), and this singleton is a basis.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-6x+y \\ 12x-2y\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 12 & -2\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 12 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=\frac{1}{6}y.
$$

 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{aligned}]y,\,y\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4x-2y \\ -6x+3y\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{6}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}y.
$$

  

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}y \\ y\end{aligned}]=y[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[4−2−63].

Setting x=[xy], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[4−2−63]R2:=R2+64R1∼[4−200]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x, and we have one free variable, y. That means we need to find x in terms of y.

Therefore, if x∈Ker(T), then

x=[12yy]=y[121],y∈R.

This implies that B={[121]} is a basis of Ker(T).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4x-2y \\ -6x+3y\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{6}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}y.
$$

  

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}y \\ y\end{aligned}]=y[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

Question 15
?

Find a basis of Ker(T) given that T:[xyz]⟶[3y−6z−6x−4y+x+z2y+8z+8x].

{[210]}
b

c

e
{[110],[0−21]}

decision.explanation: The first kernel equation gives y=2(x+z), while the second gives x+z=4y. Combining them yields y=8y, so y=0 and x=-z. These values also satisfy the third equation. Thus the kernel is spanned by the nonzero vector (-1,0,1), which forms a basis.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-6z-6x \\ -4y+x+z \\ 2y+8z+8x\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{12}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

Question 15

Find a basis of Ker(T) given that T:[xyz]⟶[3y−6z−6x−4y+x+z2y+8z+8x].

a
{[210]}
b
{[−10−3]}
c
{[−101]}
d
{[−12−31]}
e
{[110],[0−21]}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[−63−61−41828].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−63−61−41828]R2:=R2+16R1∼[−63−60−720828]R3:=R3+43R1∼[−63−60−720060]R3:=R3+127R2∼[−63−60−720000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we have x=−z.

Therefore, if x∈Ker(T), then

x=[−z0z]=[−101]z,z∈R.

This implies that B={[−101]} is a basis of Ker(T).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-6z-6x \\ -4y+x+z \\ 2y+8z+8x\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{12}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

decision.explanation: The second output is -2 times the first, so the matrix has rank 1. With two input variables, nullity(T)=2-1=1. Therefore 2·nullity(T)-3=2-3=-1.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x-8y \\ 16y-6x\end{aligned}],$
find  $2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $2$nd one). 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3=2\cdot 1-3=-1.
$$

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-z \\ x-y+z \\ 3z-6x\end{aligned}],$ find $\text{nullity}(T).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & \frac{3}{2} \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $3$rd one). Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.
$$

$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

$$

$$

First, we write down the standard matrix of T: T=[−3−62−4]

Recall that nullity(T)=nullity(T)=dim(Null(T)).

In order to find dim(Null(T)), we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−3−62−4]R2:=R2+23R1∼[−3−60−8]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
content.problem: Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-3x-6y \\ 2x-4y\end{aligned}],$ find $9\cdot \text{nullity}(T)+4.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -6 \\ 0 & -8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot column. 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=0.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
9\cdot \text{nullity}(T)+4=9\cdot 0+4=4.
$$

after.problem:
Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}5x-7y \\ 14y-10x\end{aligned}],$
find  $3\cdot \text{nullity}(T)+1.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -10 & 14\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -10 & 14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $2$nd one). 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
3\cdot \text{nullity}(T)+1=3\cdot 1+1=4.
$$
